region_note: Written for irrigated forage systems of the Great Basin (cold desert, about 1,800 m). Do not reuse the crop calendars elsewhere without local review.

market.label: Only crops with buyers I already have

references.FAO56: Allen, R.G., Pereira, L.S., Raes, D., Smith, M. (1998). Crop evapotranspiration: guidelines for computing crop water requirements. FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 (Tables 11, 12, 17 and 22).
references.FAO33: Doorenbos, J., Kassam, A.H. (1979). Yield response to water. FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 33 (yield response factor Ky); updated in Steduto et al. (2012), FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 66.
references.FAO29: Ayers, R.S., Westcot, D.W. (1985). Water quality for agriculture. FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 29, Table 4 (crop salt tolerance, after Maas & Hoffman 1977).
references.SARE: Clark, A. (ed.) (2007). Managing Cover Crops Profitably, 3rd edition. Sustainable Agriculture Research and Education (SARE) Handbook Series 9.
references.UC3512: Summers, C.G., Putnam, D.H. (eds.) (2008). Irrigated Alfalfa Management for Mediterranean and Desert Zones. University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources Publication 3512.
references.AUTOTOX: Extension guidance on alfalfa autotoxicity: University of Minnesota Extension ('allow at least one year between terminating an old alfalfa stand and reseeding'); Oklahoma State University Extension, 'Alfalfa Autotoxicity: A Good Reason to Rotate Alfalfa Fields'; University of Wisconsin Extension, 'Understanding autotoxicity in alfalfa'.
references.UNR_TEF: Davison, J. (2005). Tef Demonstration Planting Results for 2004. University of Nevada, Reno Extension Fact Sheet FS-05-28, and related UNR Extension tef fact sheets and news releases (reported irrigation ranges from about one third of alfalfa's to 2.7-3.7 acre-feet per acre: the spread is itself a finding).
references.NRCS_WIND: USDA NRCS National Agronomy Manual, Part 502 (Wind Erosion): wind erodibility groups (WEG) and soil erodibility index I.
references.RUSLE: Renard, K.G. et al. (1997). Predicting Soil Erosion by Water: RUSLE. USDA Agriculture Handbook 703 (cover-management concept: soil is protected in proportion to canopy and residue cover when erosive weather arrives).
references.NEH623: USDA NRCS National Engineering Handbook, Part 623, Chapter 2: Irrigation Water Requirements (USDA-SCS effective precipitation method).
references.PROJECT: Class score assigned by this project from the general agronomy cited alongside it; not locally calibrated.

water.label: Save water
water.plain: Lower irrigation need across the whole rotation.

cover.label: Keep soil covered
cover.plain: Plants or residue on the ground when wind and hard rain arrive.

nitrogen.label: Nitrogen from legumes
nitrogen.plain: Nitrogen fixed by legumes and used by the next crop.

organic_matter.label: Build organic matter
organic_matter.plain: Roots and residue returned to the soil, with little tillage.

pest_break.label: Break pest cycles
pest_break.plain: Different plant families and a real break between alfalfa stands.

income.label: Forage and income
income.plain: Forage value relative to established alfalfa, given your water and market.

resilience.label: Drought and heat resilience
resilience.plain: Crops that cope with hot spells and short water.

feasibility.label: Easy to carry out
feasibility.plain: Fits your season, your equipment and your experience.

why.kc: FAO56 Table 12: alfalfa hay, averaged over cutting cycles, Kc mid 0.95; lower in April and October when growth starts and ends around frost at this elevation (PROJECT).
why.cover: Perennial canopy from spring to autumn; crowns and stubble still protect the surface in winter (RUSLE cover concept; PROJECT class values).
why.n_score: Legume: fixes its own nitrogen. Credit to the following crop commonly 80-170 kg N/ha after a stand is taken out (SARE; UC3512).
why.om_score: Large perennial root system and several years without tillage, but nearly all top growth leaves the field as hay (UC3512; PROJECT).
why.root_depth_m: FAO56 Table 22: maximum effective rooting depth 1.0-3.0 m for alfalfa.
why.heat_limit_c: Cool-season legume: growth and forage quality fall off above roughly 30-35 °C ('summer slump', UC3512). 32 °C is used as the stress line.
why.drought_tolerance: Deep roots and the ability to go dormant and survive a dry spell, but yield falls in step with water (Ky 1.1, FAO33).
why.value_score: Reference crop for the valley: established hay market and equipment. All other value scores are relative to this.
why.salt_threshold_ds_m: FAO29 Table 4: yield starts to fall above ECe 2.0 dS/m.

why.kc: FAO56 Table 12 initial Kc 0.40 for alfalfa, rising to the established-stand value once the canopy closes (PROJECT monthly shape for a spring seeding).
why.cover: Bare seedbed in April-May, the windiest part of the year, until the canopy closes.
why.value_score: Seeding-year hay yield is commonly about half of an established stand (UC3512).
why.establishment_risk: Small-seeded, shallow-sown crop: wind, crusting, frost and, after old alfalfa, autotoxicity can all thin a new stand (UC3512; AUTOTOX).
why.drought_tolerance: Seedlings have shallow roots and cannot be allowed to dry out.

winter_cereal_forage.label: Winter cereal for hay (triticale, winter wheat or rye)

why.kc: FAO56 Table 12: winter wheat Kc mid 1.15, initial 0.4-0.7; cut for hay around heading so the high-demand grain-fill period is skipped (PROJECT calendar: sown September, cut late June).
why.cover: Green cover from October to June, including the windy spring; stubble afterwards (SARE).
why.om_score: Dense fibrous roots; top growth removed as hay (SARE).
why.heat_limit_c: Cool-season cereal; harvested before midsummer heat, which is the point of using it.
why.drought_tolerance: Grows on winter and spring moisture and finishes before peak summer demand (drought escape); Ky about 1.05 (FAO33, winter wheat).
why.value_score: Cereal hay sells into the same hay market at a lower price and tonnage than alfalfa (PROJECT class score; no local prices in this tool).
why.salt_threshold_ds_m: FAO29 Table 4: wheat 6.0 dS/m, triticale 6.1, rye 11.4.

why.kc: No FAO56 entry for teff; millet is used as the analogue (FAO56 Table 12: Kc mid 1.00, initial 0.30). Nevada trial figures for irrigation vary widely (UNR_TEF), so this is a LOW-confidence value.
why.cover: Fast summer canopy; fine stubble is left over winter.
why.root_depth_m: Shallow fibrous root system (FAO56 Table 22 millet 1.0-2.0 m; teff is finer and shallower, PROJECT).
why.heat_limit_c: Warm-season (C4) grass from the Ethiopian highlands: tolerates heat that stresses alfalfa.
why.drought_tolerance: Short season and C4 water-use efficiency; Ky taken as 0.9 by analogy with sorghum (FAO33).
why.frost_free_days_needed: Killed by frost. Roughly 45-55 days from sowing to a first cut and warm soil at sowing, so about 75 frost-free days are needed for one good cut and about 100 for two (UNR_TEF; PROJECT).
why.value_score: Fine-stemmed hay with a horse-hay market, but buyers are few and local (UNR_TEF): a niche market.
why.establishment_risk: Tiny seed sown very shallow into a firm seedbed; stands fail if the surface dries or crusts (UNR_TEF).

why.kc: FAO56 Table 12: Sudan grass hay (annual), averaged cutting effects, Kc mid 0.90, initial 0.50.
why.drought_tolerance: Sorghum Ky 0.9 (FAO33): one of the more drought-tolerant summer forages.
why.frost_free_days_needed: Needs warm soil and about 100 frost-free days for two cuts; frosted regrowth also carries a prussic-acid risk for livestock (SARE).
why.om_score: High biomass and a deep, fibrous root system (SARE).

why.kc: FAO56 Table 12: barley and oats Kc mid 1.15, initial 0.30; cut for hay in early July (PROJECT calendar: sown April).
why.cover: Bare seedbed in April; stubble only from mid-July unless a cover crop follows.
why.root_depth_m: FAO56 Table 22: barley and oats 1.0-1.5 m.
why.drought_tolerance: Spring cereals are sensitive to water shortage at heading (Ky about 1.15, FAO33) but finish before late-summer heat.
why.value_score: The familiar, low-risk break crop in western alfalfa systems (AUTOTOX), with a modest hay value.

spring_grain.label: Spring small grain for grain (barley or spring wheat)

why.kc: FAO56 Table 12: barley, oats and spring wheat Kc mid 1.15, end 0.25-0.4.
why.om_score: Straw and stubble stay on the field when only the grain is taken (SARE).
why.heat_limit_c: Heat above about 30 °C during grain fill cuts yield in cool-season cereals.

why.kc: FAO56 Table 12: safflower Kc mid 1.0-1.15, initial 0.35, end 0.25. NOTE: fully irrigated safflower is not a low-water crop; its reputation comes from surviving on stored soil water.
why.root_depth_m: FAO56 Table 22: 1.0-2.0 m; a taproot that can draw on moisture below most forage roots.
why.drought_tolerance: Ky 0.8 (FAO33): yield falls less than water does, which is what makes deliberate under-irrigation workable.
why.frost_free_days_needed: A long-season crop (about 120-150 days sowing to harvest). Seedlings tolerate frost; 110 days is the PROJECT minimum for the frost-sensitive stem-elongation-to-flowering period plus ripening.
why.value_score: An oilseed needs a buyer and an elevator within hauling distance; none is assumed here (PROJECT). This is the largest information gap for this crop.
why.salt_class: FAO29 Table 4 lists safflower as moderately tolerant without a threshold value.

cover_mix.label: Winter cover crop mix (cereal + winter pea or vetch)

why.kc: Treated as a small-grain canopy (FAO56 Table 12 cereals) until it is terminated in May. It uses real water: in a dry climate a cover crop is not free (SARE).
why.cover: Green cover through winter and the windy spring; a mulch after termination (SARE).
why.n_score: The legume part fixes nitrogen: SARE reports roughly 30-110 kg N/ha or more for winter peas and hairy vetch depending on growth before termination.
why.om_score: All growth is returned to the soil (SARE).
why.value_score: No sale crop; some grazing value where livestock are available.

traits.salt_class: varies by species (tall wheatgrass tolerant, orchardgrass sensitive)

why.kc: FAO56 Table 12: grass hay and rotated pasture Kc 0.85-1.05.
why.om_score: Dense perennial sod and fibrous roots, no tillage (SARE).
why.drought_tolerance: Cool-season grasses slow down or go dormant in summer heat and drought (PROJECT).

why.kc: No irrigation is applied; evaporation is met by rain.
why.cover: Sparse weeds and old residue only: the soil is largely exposed (RUSLE).
why.om_score: No living roots and no residue returned.

why.kc: Generic irrigated field crop (FAO56 Table 12 mid-range). Used only when the crop map and the greenness record disagree about what grew.
why.value_score: Neutral placeholder. Correct the crop history to replace it.

cereal_teff_break.name: Alfalfa with a two-year double-crop forage break
cereal_teff_break.summary: Five years of alfalfa, then two years in which a winter cereal cut for hay in June is followed by teff in the summer, before alfalfa is sown again.
benefits: Keeps the field producing forage in every year, with two crops in each break year.
A two-year gap between alfalfa stands meets the usual autotoxicity guidance.
The winter cereal keeps the soil covered through the windy spring.
The cereal and teff can use nitrogen left by the alfalfa.
risks: Teff stands fail easily: tiny seed, shallow sowing, and no frost tolerance.
Two sowings a year in the break years: more field work and a tight June turnaround.
Double-cropping uses almost as much water as alfalfa: this is not a water-saving option.
Herbicides used in alfalfa can carry over and injure the following crops.
Teff and cereal hay need buyers; the teff market is small.
info_gaps: Local teff and cereal-hay prices and buyers.
Teff water use here: published Nevada figures disagree widely.
Whether your frost-free season is long enough for teff in a cool year.
verify: Ask Extension or a neighbour who has grown teff at this elevation about sowing date and stand success.
Check plant-back intervals on the labels of the herbicides used in the alfalfa.
Line up a hay buyer before sowing teff.
Confirm how your water right or allocation treats a split-season crop.

safflower_cover.name: Alfalfa with a deep-rooted crop and a winter cover crop
safflower_cover.summary: Five years of alfalfa, then a year of safflower followed by a winter cover crop mix, then spring grain hay, before alfalfa is sown again.
benefits: A taproot crop from a different plant family breaks alfalfa pest and disease cycles.
The cover crop protects the soil over winter and spring and returns all its growth to the soil.
Safflower tolerates being under-irrigated better than alfalfa.
risks: Fully irrigated safflower uses a lot of water; savings only come if it is deliberately under-irrigated.
Needs a combine and a buyer: neither is certain here.
A long-season crop in a short frost-free season.
The cover crop uses water and has to be terminated on time.
info_gaps: Whether any safflower buyer or elevator is within hauling distance.
Safflower yield at this elevation: no local trial data in this tool.
How much stored soil water is really available below the alfalfa root zone.
verify: Ask Extension whether safflower has been grown successfully in the valley.
Get a custom-harvest quote if you do not own a combine.
Check with NRCS whether a cover crop qualifies for cost-share.
Take a deep soil-moisture or soil-test sample before relying on stored water.

short_stand_grain.name: Shorter alfalfa stands with a small-grain hay year
short_stand_grain.summary: Four years of alfalfa after the seeding year, then one year of oat or barley hay, then alfalfa again: the conventional, low-risk rotation of western alfalfa growers.
benefits: Uses the hay equipment and hay market you already have.
One year out of alfalfa reduces autotoxicity risk for the new seeding.
The grain-hay year needs less water and none in late summer.
Younger stands are usually thicker and more productive.
risks: Only a one-year break: the minimum that Extension guidance suggests.
The field is bare in April and mostly stubble from July of the grain year.
More frequent seeding costs: a seeding year yields about half.
info_gaps: The real age and condition of your current stand.
Your seeding cost and the price difference between grain hay and alfalfa.
verify: Walk the stand: count plants or stems per square foot to see if it is past its best.
Discuss with Extension whether one year is a long enough break on your soil.

water_saver.name: Short alfalfa stand with three single-crop, low-water years
water_saver.summary: Three years of alfalfa after the seeding year, then three years of one short-season forage each: winter cereal hay, then teff after a winter cover crop, then oat or barley hay. No irrigation in the gaps between them.
benefits: The lowest irrigation need of the options here: each break year grows one short-season crop.
Most of the water is used in spring, outside the July-August peak.
Wide mix of plant families and a three-year alfalfa break.
risks: Less alfalfa and single-cropped years mean clearly less forage to sell.
Stubble only in late summer and autumn of two of the break years.
Depends on teff, the least certain crop here.
info_gaps: Whether annual-forage hay can be sold in the volume this would produce.
Labour and machinery time for five sowings in seven years.
verify: Budget it with Extension enterprise sheets using your own prices.
Try the annual-forage sequence on part of one pivot first.

benefits: You know this system and already have the equipment and the buyers.
Alfalfa keeps the ground covered all year once established.
No purchased nitrogen: alfalfa fixes its own.
risks: High irrigation need in every year.
Old stands thin out, and weeds, nematodes and diseases build up.
Sowing alfalfa straight after alfalfa risks autotoxicity.
info_gaps: The crop history here comes from a satellite crop map, not from your records.
Stand age, yields and the water you actually applied.
verify: Correct the crop history if the map is wrong.
Compare the water-use estimate with your own meter or pumping records.

always_verify: Water right, allocation or groundwater-plan rules that apply to this field.
A current soil test (salinity, sodium, nutrients, organic matter).
Local seed availability and sowing dates.
Local buyers and prices for every crop that is new to you.
